histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.back: Under oestrogen (puberty/pregnancy) the original SCJ everts (ectropion) and metaplasia forms a new/functional SCJ on the ectocervix; after menopause this functional SCJ recedes into the endocervical canal.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.front: Why is the post-menopausal transformation zone harder to sample?
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.back: The squamocolumnar junction recedes into the endocervical canal, so the transformation zone becomes less accessible for smears.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.front: How does the cervix differ histologically from the uterine body?
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.back: The cervix has squamous ectocervix + glandular endocervix and a mainly fibrous stroma, whereas the uterine body has endometrial glands and a thick smooth-muscle myometrium.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.front: What glycogen-related feature characterises normal ectocervical squamous cells?
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.back: They are rich in glycogen (which is why they stain brown with iodine and support lactobacilli that keep the vagina acidic).

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.front: What are endocervical crypts?
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.back: Deep, branching infoldings of the endocervical columnar epithelium, often mistaken for true glands, that secrete mucus.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.front: What is the significance of HPV persistence versus clearance?
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.back: Most HPV infections clear spontaneously; persistent high-risk HPV infection at the TZ is what leads to CIN and cancer.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.front: Which cervical cancer type is more likely to be missed by cytology screening?
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.back: Adenocarcinoma, because it arises higher in the endocervical canal/glands away from the sampled squamous TZ.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.front: What protective role does the acidic vaginal environment play at the ectocervix?
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.back: Glycogen from squamous cells feeds lactobacilli that produce lactic acid, maintaining a low pH that suppresses pathogens.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.front: What is the difference between CIN and invasive cervical carcinoma?
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.back: CIN is dysplasia confined above the basement membrane (intra-epithelial); invasive carcinoma has breached the basement membrane into the stroma.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.front: Why is squamous metaplasia in the transformation zone a double-edged process?
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.back: It is a normal protective adaptation, but the actively dividing metaplastic cells are especially susceptible to HPV integration and malignant transformation.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.front: What are subcolumnar reserve cells?
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.back: Small bipotential stem-like cells beneath the endocervical columnar epithelium; they proliferate and differentiate into squamous epithelium (squamous metaplasia) and are the presumed origin of most cervical neoplasia.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.front: Describe the three maturation layers of ectocervical squamous epithelium.
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.back: Basal/parabasal (small dividing cells on the basement membrane) → intermediate (larger, glycogen-rich) → superficial (flat, pyknotic, shed); nuclei shrink and cytoplasm expands upward.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.front: How is CIN graded histologically?
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.back: By how far immature basal-type cells extend up the epithelium: CIN1 = lower third, CIN2 = up to two-thirds, CIN3 = full thickness (basement membrane still intact = intra-epithelial).

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.front: What is the two-tier (LSIL/HSIL) system and its CIN mapping?
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.back: LSIL = CIN1 (productive HPV, koilocytes, usually regresses); HSIL = CIN2–3 (transforming infection, true precancer, treated).

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.front: Why is p16 immunostaining useful in cervical dysplasia?
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.back: Diffuse "block" p16 positivity marks HSIL — E7 inactivation of Rb causes feedback p16 over-expression; it distinguishes true HSIL from reactive mimics (Ki-67 also extends into upper layers).

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.front: What is the acetowhite test at colposcopy?
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.back: Applying 5% acetic acid to the cervix turns dysplastic (high nuclear:cytoplasmic ratio) epithelium white (acetowhite), guiding targeted biopsy of the transformation zone.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.front: How is high-grade CIN (HSIL) treated and what is the trade-off?
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.back: Excision of the transformation zone by LLETZ/LEEP (or cold-knife cone biopsy); effective but increases the risk of later preterm birth and cervical stenosis.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.front: What is the modern primary cervical screening test?
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.back: Primary high-risk HPV testing (with reflex cytology if HPV-positive), which is more sensitive than cytology alone — and better detects HPV-positive adenocarcinoma.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Testis (seminif.question: Which two features identify the testis histologically?
options: Seminiferous tubules and interstitial Leydig cells
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Testis (seminif.explanation: Seminiferous tubules with a stratified germinal epithelium plus interstitial Leydig cells are diagnostic of the testis.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Testis (seminif.question: Within the seminiferous epithelium, germ cells mature:
options: From the base (spermatogonia) toward the lumen (spermatozoa)
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Testis (seminif.explanation: Spermatogenesis proceeds from spermatogonia at the base to spermatozoa released at the lumen.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Testis (seminif.question: The largest, most conspicuous germ cells in the tubule are the:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Testis (seminif.explanation: Primary spermatocytes are the largest germ cells, with prominent condensed chromatin as they undergo meiosis I.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Testis (seminif.question: The blood–testis barrier is formed by:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Testis (seminif.explanation: Sertoli–Sertoli tight junctions create the blood–testis barrier, dividing basal and adluminal compartments.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Testis (seminif.question: Which pituitary hormone acts on Sertoli cells?
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Testis (seminif.explanation: FSH acts on Sertoli cells; LH acts on Leydig cells.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Testis (seminif.question: Leydig cells secrete ______ under the control of ______.
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Testis (seminif.explanation: Leydig (interstitial) cells produce testosterone in response to LH.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Testis (seminif.question: Rod-shaped cytoplasmic crystals characteristic of Leydig cells are called:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Testis (seminif.explanation: Reinke crystals are characteristic cytoplasmic inclusions of Leydig cells.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Testis (seminif.question: Androgen-binding protein (ABP), secreted by Sertoli cells, functions to:
options: Keep intratubular testosterone high to support spermatogenesis
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Testis (seminif.explanation: ABP binds testosterone to maintain a high local concentration within the seminiferous tubules.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Testis (seminif.question: Inhibin from Sertoli cells provides negative feedback on:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Testis (seminif.explanation: Inhibin selectively suppresses FSH secretion from the anterior pituitary.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Testis (seminif.question: The epididymis is lined by:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Testis (seminif.explanation: The epididymis has a pseudostratified columnar epithelium bearing long stereocilia, where sperm mature and are stored.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Testis (seminif.question: The straight tubules (tubuli recti) are lined by:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Testis (seminif.explanation: Tubuli recti are lined by Sertoli cells only and connect the seminiferous tubules to the rete testis.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Testis (seminif.question: The efferent ductules characteristically:
options: Reabsorb testicular fluid and show a scalloped lining
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Testis (seminif.explanation: Efferent ductules reabsorb most testicular fluid; alternating tall ciliated and short cells give a scalloped luminal outline.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Testis (seminif.question: Cryptorchidism (undescended testis) is associated with:
options: Impaired spermatogenesis and increased germ-cell tumour risk
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Testis (seminif.explanation: An undescended testis has impaired spermatogenesis and a higher risk of germ-cell tumours.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Testis (seminif.question: The commonest testicular germ-cell tumour, showing 'fried-egg' cells and a lymphocytic stroma, is:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Testis (seminif.explanation: Seminoma is the commonest germ-cell tumour: sheets of clear 'fried-egg' cells with a lymphocytic infiltrate.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Testis (seminif.question: A raised alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) suggests which testicular tumour component?
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Testis (seminif.explanation: Yolk-sac (endodermal sinus) tumour raises AFP; choriocarcinoma raises beta-hCG.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Testis (seminif.question: The testicular histology of Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) shows:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Testis (seminif.explanation: Klinefelter testes are small and firm with hyalinised, fibrosed seminiferous tubules and Leydig-cell hyperplasia, causing infertility.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Testis (seminif.question: Sertoli-cell-only syndrome causes azoospermia because:
options: Tubules contain Sertoli cells but no germ cells
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Testis (seminif.explanation: In Sertoli-cell-only syndrome (germ-cell aplasia) tubules are lined by Sertoli cells only, so no sperm are produced.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Testis (seminif.question: A left-sided 'bag of worms' scrotal swelling that may impair fertility is a:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Testis (seminif.explanation: A varicocele is dilatation of the pampiniform plexus, usually left-sided, and can impair fertility.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Testis (seminif.question: Breach of the blood–testis barrier can lead to:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Testis (seminif.explanation: The barrier hides haploid germ-cell antigens; if breached (trauma/vasectomy/infection), anti-sperm antibodies may form.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Testis (seminif.question: Which statement correctly pairs a cell with its hormone control?
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Testis (seminif.explanation: Leydig cells respond to LH (making testosterone); Sertoli cells respond to FSH.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Testis (seminif.question: A raised serum alpha-fetoprotein in a man with a testicular germ-cell tumour indicates:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Testis (seminif.explanation: Pure seminoma NEVER raises AFP; a raised AFP proves a non-seminomatous germ-cell (yolk-sac) component, which changes staging and treatment. Choriocarcinoma raises beta-hCG.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Testis (seminif.question: Immotile spermatozoa and fluid are propelled along the seminiferous tubule toward the rete testis by:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Testis (seminif.explanation: Contractile peritubular myoid cells ringing the tubule generate the peristalsis that moves immotile sperm (which gain motility only later, in the epididymis) and fluid toward the rete testis.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Ovary (follicle.question: Which feature identifies the ovary histologically?
options: A cortex containing follicles at various stages
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Ovary (follicle.explanation: The ovarian cortex packed with follicles at different developmental stages is diagnostic.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Ovary (follicle.question: A primordial follicle consists of an oocyte surrounded by:
options: A single layer of flat (squamous) follicular cells
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Ovary (follicle.explanation: Primordial follicles have a single layer of flat follicular cells around the primary oocyte.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Ovary (follicle.question: The zona pellucida first appears at which stage and is composed of:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Ovary (follicle.explanation: The glycoprotein zona pellucida appears as the follicle becomes a primary follicle and mediates sperm binding.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Ovary (follicle.question: The defining feature of a secondary (antral) follicle is:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Ovary (follicle.explanation: A fluid-filled antrum appearing among the granulosa cells marks the secondary (antral) follicle.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Ovary (follicle.question: In the two-cell model, theca interna cells respond to ______ and produce ______.
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Ovary (follicle.explanation: Theca interna cells respond to LH and produce androgens, which the granulosa cells aromatise to oestrogen.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Ovary (follicle.question: Granulosa cells respond to FSH by producing ______ via aromatase.
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Ovary (follicle.explanation: FSH induces aromatase in granulosa cells, converting theca-derived androgens into oestrogen.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Ovary (follicle.question: Ovulation is triggered by:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Ovary (follicle.explanation: The mid-cycle LH surge triggers ovulation of the secondary oocyte from the Graafian follicle.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Ovary (follicle.question: The corpus luteum principally secretes:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Ovary (follicle.explanation: The corpus luteum's lutein cells secrete progesterone (with oestrogen) to maintain the endometrium.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Ovary (follicle.question: If pregnancy does not occur, the corpus luteum becomes a:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Ovary (follicle.explanation: Without pregnancy the corpus luteum regresses after ~14 days into a white fibrous corpus albicans.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Ovary (follicle.question: The corpus luteum is maintained in early pregnancy by:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Ovary (follicle.explanation: hCG produced by the trophoblast rescues the corpus luteum until the placenta assumes hormone production.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Ovary (follicle.question: At ovulation, the oocyte is arrested in:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Ovary (follicle.explanation: The ovulated secondary oocyte is arrested in metaphase II and only completes meiosis II if fertilised.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Ovary (follicle.question: Call–Exner bodies are characteristically seen in:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Ovary (follicle.explanation: Call–Exner bodies (granulosa cells around eosinophilic material) are typical of antral follicles and granulosa cell tumours.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Ovary (follicle.question: The commonest epithelial ovarian tumour, associated with psammoma bodies and raised CA-125, is:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Ovary (follicle.explanation: Serous tumours are the commonest ovarian epithelial neoplasm and characteristically show psammoma bodies with raised CA-125.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Ovary (follicle.question: A granulosa cell tumour typically secretes ______ and can cause ______.
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Ovary (follicle.explanation: Granulosa cell tumours secrete oestrogen (and inhibin), causing precocious puberty or endometrial hyperplasia/bleeding.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Ovary (follicle.question: Meigs syndrome is the association of an ovarian fibroma with:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Ovary (follicle.explanation: Meigs syndrome is an ovarian fibroma with ascites and pleural effusion that resolve after tumour removal.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Ovary (follicle.question: A benign ovarian tumour containing hair, skin and teeth is a:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Ovary (follicle.explanation: A mature cystic teratoma (dermoid) contains derivatives of all three germ layers such as hair, skin and teeth.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Ovary (follicle.question: Polycystic ovary syndrome shows which ovarian histology?
options: Multiple peripheral (subcapsular) follicular cysts with a thickened tunica
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Ovary (follicle.explanation: PCOS shows many subcapsular follicular cysts and a thickened tunica albuginea with arrested follicles and anovulation.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Ovary (follicle.question: The ovarian germ-cell tumour equivalent to the testicular seminoma is the:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Ovary (follicle.explanation: The dysgerminoma is the ovarian counterpart of the seminoma; it may raise LDH and hCG.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Ovary (follicle.question: Which marker is characteristically produced by a granulosa cell tumour?
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Ovary (follicle.explanation: Granulosa cell tumours characteristically secrete inhibin (and oestrogen).

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Ovary (follicle.question: An ovarian 'chocolate cyst' filled with old blood is a(n):
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Ovary (follicle.explanation: An endometrioma is an ovarian cyst of endometriosis containing altered old blood, giving a chocolate-coloured fluid.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Ovary (follicle.question: From fetal life until ovulation, primary oocytes are arrested in:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Ovary (follicle.explanation: Primary oocytes arrest in prophase I (dictyate) from fetal life; the LH surge completes meiosis I just before ovulation, producing a secondary oocyte that then arrests in metaphase II until fertilisation.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Ovary (follicle.question: Bilateral ovarian masses of mucin-filled signet-ring cells in a woman with gastric cancer are a:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Ovary (follicle.explanation: A Krukenberg tumour is bilateral ovarian metastasis of signet-ring cells, classically from a gastric (or colonic) adenocarcinoma spreading transcoelomically.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Uterus (endomet.question: Which finding identifies a slide as uterus (endometrium)?
options: Endometrial glands in a cellular stroma over a thick myometrium
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Uterus (endomet.explanation: Endometrial glands set in a cellular stroma over a thick smooth-muscle myometrium identify the uterus.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Uterus (endomet.question: The stratum functionalis of the endometrium is:
options: The layer that regenerates the endometrium
The superficial layer shed at menstruation
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Uterus (endomet.explanation: The functionalis is the superficial layer, shed each menstruation and rebuilt from the basalis.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Uterus (endomet.question: The functionalis is supplied by which vessels?
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Uterus (endomet.explanation: Spiral arteries supply the functionalis and constrict on hormone withdrawal to cause menstruation.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Uterus (endomet.question: In the proliferative phase, the endometrial glands are:
options: Straight, narrow and tubular with many mitoses
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Uterus (endomet.explanation: Oestrogen-driven proliferation gives straight tubular glands with abundant mitoses.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Uterus (endomet.question: The proliferative phase is driven by:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Uterus (endomet.explanation: Oestrogen from the developing follicles drives endometrial proliferation.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Uterus (endomet.question: The secretory phase is driven by ______, produced by the ______.
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Uterus (endomet.explanation: Progesterone from the corpus luteum drives the secretory phase after ovulation.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Uterus (endomet.question: The first histological sign that ovulation has occurred is:
options: Sub-nuclear glycogen vacuoles in gland cells (~day 16–17)
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Uterus (endomet.explanation: Sub-nuclear glycogen vacuoles appearing around day 16–17 are the earliest sign of ovulation (progesterone effect).

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Uterus (endomet.question: Coiled 'sawtooth' glands with luminal secretions and stromal oedema indicate the ______ phase.
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Uterus (endomet.explanation: Coiled sawtooth glands, glycogen/secretions and stromal oedema are hallmarks of the secretory (luteal) phase.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Uterus (endomet.question: Menstruation is directly triggered by:
options: Spiral-artery constriction due to falling progesterone/oestrogen
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Uterus (endomet.explanation: As the corpus luteum regresses, hormone withdrawal causes spiral arteries to constrict, producing ischaemic shedding.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Uterus (endomet.question: Which layer regenerates the endometrium after menstruation?
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Uterus (endomet.explanation: The retained stratum basalis regenerates the functionalis each cycle.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Uterus (endomet.question: Endometrial hyperplasia is most often caused by:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Uterus (endomet.explanation: Unopposed oestrogen (without progesterone) drives endometrial hyperplasia, which may progress to carcinoma.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Uterus (endomet.question: The commonest presenting symptom of endometrial adenocarcinoma is:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Uterus (endomet.explanation: Endometrial carcinoma classically presents with postmenopausal bleeding.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Uterus (endomet.question: A benign whorled smooth-muscle tumour of the myometrium is a:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Uterus (endomet.explanation: A leiomyoma (fibroid) is a benign, oestrogen-dependent smooth-muscle tumour with a whorled pattern — the commonest uterine tumour.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Uterus (endomet.question: The presence of endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium is called:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Uterus (endomet.explanation: Adenomyosis is endometrial tissue within the myometrium; endometriosis is endometrial tissue outside the uterus.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Uterus (endomet.question: Fibroids (leiomyomas) are described as oestrogen-dependent because they:
options: Grow with oestrogen and often shrink after menopause
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Uterus (endomet.explanation: Leiomyomas grow under oestrogen influence and typically regress after menopause when oestrogen falls.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Uterus (endomet.question: Asherman's syndrome results from damage to the:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Uterus (endomet.explanation: Damage to the stratum basalis (e.g. aggressive curettage) causes intrauterine adhesions, amenorrhoea and infertility.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Uterus (endomet.question: Which of the following is a risk factor for endometrial carcinoma?
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Uterus (endomet.explanation: Conditions increasing unopposed oestrogen (obesity, PCOS, tamoxifen, nulliparity, late menopause, Lynch) raise endometrial cancer risk.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Uterus (endomet.question: A leiomyosarcoma is distinguished from a leiomyoma by:
options: High mitotic activity, atypia and tumour necrosis
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Uterus (endomet.explanation: Leiomyosarcoma shows high mitoses, cytological atypia and necrosis, marking it as malignant.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Uterus (endomet.question: Which vessels remain intact during menstruation to allow regeneration?
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Uterus (endomet.explanation: Straight (basal) arteries supply the retained basalis and persist through menstruation to regenerate the functionalis.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Uterus (endomet.question: Endometriosis is defined as:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Uterus (endomet.explanation: Endometriosis is functional endometrial tissue located outside the uterine cavity, causing cyclical pain and adhesions.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Uterus (endomet.question: Which pairing correctly describes the two types of endometrial carcinoma?
options: Type 1 serous / p53; Type 2 endometrioid / PTEN
Type 1 endometrioid / oestrogen-related / PTEN; Type 2 serous / p53 / aggressive
Type 2 is the commonest and low-grade
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Uterus (endomet.explanation: Type 1 (endometrioid) is oestrogen-related, arises on hyperplasia, shows PTEN loss and is low-grade; Type 2 (serous) is non-oestrogen-related, arises on atrophic endometrium, has TP53 mutation with psammoma bodies and is aggressive.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Uterus (endomet.question: The histological hallmark of chronic endometritis is:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Uterus (endomet.explanation: Chronic endometritis is defined by plasma cells in the endometrial stroma (normally absent); causes include retained products of conception, IUDs/Actinomyces and tuberculosis.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Fallopian Tube.question: Which feature identifies the fallopian tube histologically?
options: Labyrinthine mucosal folds with ciliated and peg cells, no glands
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Fallopian Tube.explanation: Elaborate branching mucosal folds lined by ciliated and peg cells, without glands, identify the fallopian tube (especially the ampulla).

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Fallopian Tube.question: The two epithelial cell types of the fallopian tube are:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Fallopian Tube.explanation: The tubal epithelium contains ciliated cells (transport) and secretory 'peg' cells (nutrition).

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Fallopian Tube.question: The cilia of the fallopian tube beat:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Fallopian Tube.explanation: Ciliary beating is directed toward the uterus, moving the oocyte and embryo along the tube.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Fallopian Tube.question: Ciliation of the tubal epithelium is increased by:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Fallopian Tube.explanation: Oestrogen promotes ciliation and taller cells; progesterone favours secretion and deciliation.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Fallopian Tube.question: Fertilisation normally occurs in the:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Fallopian Tube.explanation: The ampulla, the longest and most folded region, is the usual site of fertilisation.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Fallopian Tube.question: The finger-like projections that capture the ovulated oocyte are the:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Fallopian Tube.explanation: Fimbriae at the infundibulum sweep over the ovary to catch the oocyte at ovulation.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Fallopian Tube.question: Which region of the tube has the most elaborate mucosal folds?
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Fallopian Tube.explanation: Mucosal folds are most complex in the ampulla and become simpler toward the isthmus.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Fallopian Tube.question: The commonest site of an ectopic pregnancy is the:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Fallopian Tube.explanation: Most tubal ectopic pregnancies implant in the ampulla, often after scarring or ciliary dysfunction delays transport.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Fallopian Tube.question: Secretory (peg) cells of the fallopian tube:
options: Secrete nutritive fluid and aid sperm capacitation
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Fallopian Tube.explanation: Peg cells secrete fluid that nourishes gametes/embryo and helps capacitate sperm; they bulge into the lumen.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Fallopian Tube.question: The muscularis of the fallopian tube consists of:
options: Inner circular and outer longitudinal smooth muscle
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Fallopian Tube.explanation: The tube has an inner circular and outer longitudinal smooth-muscle layer whose peristalsis aids transport.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Fallopian Tube.question: Pelvic inflammatory disease damages the tube leading to:
options: Scarring with infertility and ectopic risk
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Fallopian Tube.explanation: PID scars the tube, causing infertility, ectopic pregnancy risk and hydrosalpinx.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Fallopian Tube.question: A fallopian tube distended with clear fluid after chronic inflammation is a:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Fallopian Tube.explanation: A hydrosalpinx is a blocked tube distended with clear serous fluid following chronic inflammation.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Fallopian Tube.question: Serous tubal intra-epithelial carcinoma (STIC) arises at the ______ and is a precursor of ______.
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Fallopian Tube.explanation: STIC at the fimbrial end (with p53 mutation) is now recognised as the origin of most high-grade serous carcinomas.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Fallopian Tube.question: Which molecular abnormality is characteristic of STIC?
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Fallopian Tube.explanation: TP53 (p53) mutations characterise serous tubal intra-epithelial carcinoma and high-grade serous carcinoma.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Fallopian Tube.question: Primary ciliary dyskinesia (Kartagener syndrome) affects fertility by:
options: Impairing ciliary oocyte transport, causing subfertility and ectopic risk
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Fallopian Tube.explanation: Defective cilia impair transport of the oocyte, causing subfertility and increased ectopic pregnancy risk.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Fallopian Tube.question: Compared with the ampulla, the isthmus has:
options: More elaborate folds and thinner muscle
Fewer folds and a thicker muscular wall
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Fallopian Tube.explanation: The isthmus is narrow with fewer mucosal folds and a thicker muscular wall than the ampulla.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Fallopian Tube.question: The fallopian tube differs from the endometrium in that it:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Fallopian Tube.explanation: The tube has folded mucosa with surface ciliated/peg cells but no glands or submucosa, unlike the endometrium.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Fallopian Tube.question: Which structure funnels the ovulated oocyte into the tube?
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Fallopian Tube.explanation: The funnel-shaped infundibulum with its fimbriae captures the oocyte at ovulation.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Fallopian Tube.question: Tubal ligation achieves contraception by:
options: Dividing or occluding the fallopian tubes
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Fallopian Tube.explanation: Tubal ligation surgically divides or occludes the tubes, preventing oocyte–sperm meeting.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Fallopian Tube.question: Oocyte transport along the tube depends on:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Fallopian Tube.explanation: Both ciliary beating (toward the uterus) and peristalsis of the muscularis move the oocyte along the tube.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Fallopian Tube.question: Which ectopic pregnancy site, though less common, is the most dangerous because it ruptures late and catastrophically?
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Fallopian Tube.explanation: The interstitial (intramural/cornual) ectopic is surrounded by myometrium, so it grows larger before rupturing - causing late, catastrophic haemorrhage. The ampulla is the commonest site overall.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Fallopian Tube.question: Serous tubal intra-epithelial carcinoma at the fimbrial end is most strongly associated with:
options: BRCA1/2 germline mutation and a TP53 signature
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Fallopian Tube.explanation: STIC carries a TP53 mutation ('p53 signature') and is strongly linked to BRCA1/2; recognising the tube as the origin of high-grade serous carcinoma underpins risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy in BRCA carriers.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Placenta.question: The human placenta is classified as ______ because maternal blood directly bathes the villous trophoblast.
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Placenta.explanation: In a haemochorial placenta, maternal blood directly contacts the syncytiotrophoblast of the villi; blood does not mix.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Placenta.question: Which structure identifies the placenta histologically?
options: Chorionic villi in a maternal-blood-filled intervillous space
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Placenta.explanation: Chorionic villi suspended in an intervillous space bathed by maternal blood are diagnostic of placenta.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Placenta.question: The outer trophoblast layer that contacts maternal blood and makes hormones is the:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Placenta.explanation: The multinucleated syncytiotrophoblast forms the outer surface, performing exchange and hormone synthesis.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Placenta.question: The cytotrophoblast (Langhans cells) functions as:
options: Mitotic stem cells replenishing the syncytiotrophoblast
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Placenta.explanation: Cytotrophoblast cells are stem cells that proliferate and fuse to maintain the syncytiotrophoblast; they diminish with gestation.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Placenta.question: Hofbauer cells in the villous core are:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Placenta.explanation: Hofbauer cells are fetal macrophages within the villous core.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Placenta.question: How does the placental barrier change toward term?
options: It thins as cytotrophoblast disappears and membranes fuse
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Placenta.explanation: By term the barrier thins — cytotrophoblast largely disappears and basement membranes fuse — improving diffusion.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Placenta.question: The umbilical cord normally contains:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Placenta.explanation: The cord has two umbilical arteries (deoxygenated) and one umbilical vein (oxygenated) in Wharton's jelly.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Placenta.question: The umbilical vein carries:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Placenta.explanation: The single umbilical vein returns oxygenated, nutrient-rich blood from the placenta to the fetus.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Placenta.question: Maternal blood enters the intervillous space from the:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Placenta.explanation: Maternal spiral arteries open into the intervillous space to bathe the villi; blood drains via endometrial veins.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Placenta.question: Failure of trophoblastic remodelling of the spiral arteries causes:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Placenta.explanation: Inadequate spiral-artery remodelling under-perfuses the placenta, causing pre-eclampsia and IUGR.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Placenta.question: Which hormone maintains the corpus luteum in early pregnancy?
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Placenta.explanation: hCG from the syncytiotrophoblast maintains the corpus luteum until the placenta takes over hormone production.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Placenta.question: Human placental lactogen (hPL) contributes to gestational diabetes by:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Placenta.explanation: hPL induces maternal insulin resistance to divert glucose to the fetus, predisposing to gestational diabetes.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Placenta.question: Wharton's jelly is:
options: The mucoid connective tissue cushioning the umbilical vessels
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Placenta.explanation: Wharton's jelly is the mucoid connective tissue of the cord that protects the umbilical vessels.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Placenta.question: Placenta accreta occurs because of:
options: Absent or deficient decidua allowing villi to invade the myometrium
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Placenta.explanation: Deficient decidua lets villi adhere to/invade the myometrium (accreta/increta/percreta), risking severe haemorrhage.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Placenta.question: A complete hydatidiform mole is characterised by:
options: An entirely paternal genome (46,XX), no fetus, diffuse villous oedema and very high hCG
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Placenta.explanation: A complete mole is androgenetic (46,XX, all paternal), has no fetus, shows diffuse villous swelling and markedly raised hCG.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Placenta.question: A partial hydatidiform mole is typically:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Placenta.explanation: A partial mole is triploid, contains some fetal tissue, and shows focal villous swelling with milder trophoblast proliferation.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Placenta.question: Choriocarcinoma characteristically:
options: Secretes AFP and spreads to bone
Secretes hCG and spreads haematogenously to the lungs
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Placenta.explanation: Choriocarcinoma is malignant trophoblast that secretes hCG and metastasises haematogenously, classically to the lungs; it lacks villi.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Placenta.question: Rhesus haemolytic disease of the newborn results from:
options: Maternal anti-D IgG crossing the placenta to haemolyse fetal red cells
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Placenta.explanation: Maternal anti-D antibodies cross the placenta and haemolyse Rh-positive fetal red cells (erythroblastosis fetalis).

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Placenta.question: A single umbilical artery is clinically important because it is associated with:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Placenta.explanation: A single umbilical artery is associated with congenital malformations, particularly renal and cardiac.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Placenta.question: Which layer of the villus performs both hormone synthesis and materno-fetal transport?
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Placenta.explanation: The syncytiotrophoblast is the working surface for both hormone production and exchange with maternal blood.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Placenta.question: Maternal oestriol reflects fetal wellbeing because its synthesis requires:
options: Fetal adrenal DHEA-S plus placental aromatase (the fetoplacental unit)
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Placenta.explanation: Oestriol needs the fetoplacental unit - fetal adrenal DHEA-S, fetal-liver 16-hydroxylation and placental aromatisation - so it falls with fetal compromise. Progesterone needs only the placenta and does not indicate fetal wellbeing.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Placenta.question: Which biomarker pattern reflects the anti-angiogenic state of pre-eclampsia?
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Placenta.explanation: The ischaemic pre-eclamptic placenta releases excess soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 (sFlt-1), which sequesters placental growth factor (PlGF); a high sFlt-1/PlGF ratio supports the diagnosis. The underlying lesion is acute atherosis of the spiral arteries.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Breast (resting.question: The breast is best described as a:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Breast (resting.explanation: The breast is a modified apocrine sweat gland with a compound tubuloalveolar structure.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Breast (resting.question: The functional unit of the breast, and origin of most pathology, is the:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Breast (resting.explanation: The TDLU (terminal duct + acini) is the hormone-responsive functional unit and the source of most breast disease.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Breast (resting.question: Breast ducts and acini are lined by:
options: Two layers: inner luminal epithelial and outer myoepithelial
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Breast (resting.explanation: A two-cell layer — inner secretory luminal cells and outer contractile myoepithelial cells — lines the ducts and acini.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Breast (resting.question: Myoepithelial cells of the breast function to:
options: Contract under oxytocin to eject milk
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Breast (resting.explanation: Myoepithelial cells contract in response to oxytocin, ejecting milk (let-down).

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Breast (resting.question: The resting (non-lactating) breast is characterised histologically by:
options: Predominant fibrofatty stroma with sparse small acini
Numerous Montgomery glands in the lobules
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Breast (resting.explanation: In the resting breast, dense fibrofatty stroma predominates with only sparse, small glandular acini.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Breast (resting.question: During lactation, the breast shows:
options: Enlarged secretion-filled alveoli with reduced stroma
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Breast (resting.explanation: Lactation expands the alveoli with secretion and reduces the stroma as glands crowd it out.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Breast (resting.question: Oestrogen and progesterone act on the breast to promote, respectively:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Breast (resting.explanation: Oestrogen drives duct growth; progesterone drives lobuloalveolar (acinar) development.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Breast (resting.question: Milk synthesis is driven mainly by:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Breast (resting.explanation: Prolactin drives milk synthesis; oxytocin drives its ejection.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Breast (resting.question: Milk ejection ('let-down') is caused by:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Breast (resting.explanation: Oxytocin released on suckling contracts the myoepithelial cells, ejecting milk from the alveoli.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Breast (resting.question: Milk protein (casein) is secreted by which mechanism?
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Breast (resting.explanation: Proteins are secreted by the merocrine mode (exocytosis); milk fat is secreted by the apocrine mode.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Breast (resting.question: Milk fat is secreted by which mechanism?
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Breast (resting.explanation: Lipid is released by the apocrine mode, enveloped in apical membrane and a little cytoplasm.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Breast (resting.question: Why does copious milk secretion begin only after delivery?
options: Falling placental oestrogen/progesterone releases prolactin's action
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Breast (resting.explanation: High placental oestrogen/progesterone inhibit prolactin's secretory effect; their fall after delivery permits lactation.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Breast (resting.question: Most breast carcinomas arise from the:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Breast (resting.explanation: The TDLU is the site of origin of most breast carcinomas.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Breast (resting.question: The commonest type of invasive breast cancer is:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Breast (resting.explanation: Invasive ductal carcinoma (NST) is the commonest invasive breast cancer.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Breast (resting.question: How do pathologists distinguish DCIS from invasive carcinoma?
options: By the presence (DCIS) or loss (invasive) of the myoepithelial layer/basement membrane
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Breast (resting.explanation: An intact myoepithelial layer/basement membrane indicates DCIS; its loss around tumour cells indicates invasion.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Breast (resting.question: Invasive lobular carcinoma characteristically shows:
options: Loss of E-cadherin with single-file infiltration
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Breast (resting.explanation: Lobular carcinoma loses E-cadherin, giving discohesive 'Indian-file' infiltrating cells.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Breast (resting.question: The commonest benign breast tumour in a young woman is a:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Breast (resting.explanation: A fibroadenoma is the commonest benign breast tumour in young women — a mobile, firm 'breast mouse'.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Breast (resting.question: A bloody nipple discharge from a solitary duct is most typically caused by:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Breast (resting.explanation: An intraductal papilloma is the classic benign cause of a bloody nipple discharge.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Breast (resting.question: Lactational mastitis/abscess is usually caused by:
options: Staphylococcus aureus via a cracked nipple
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Breast (resting.explanation: Staphylococcus aureus entering through a cracked nipple during breastfeeding causes lactational mastitis/abscess.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Breast (resting.question: Breast cancers are routinely classified for treatment by:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Breast (resting.explanation: ER, PR and HER2 status guide endocrine and anti-HER2 therapy; triple-negative tumours lack all three and carry a worse prognosis.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Breast (resting.question: Lobular carcinoma in situ (LCIS) is best regarded as:
options: A non-mass-forming risk marker for cancer in both breasts
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Breast (resting.explanation: LCIS is E-cadherin-negative but does not form a mass or invade; it is often multicentric/bilateral and acts as a risk marker (raising cancer risk in both breasts) rather than a direct precursor. Invasive lobular carcinoma instead shows Indian-file infiltration.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Breast (resting.question: A large, rapidly enlarging fibroepithelial breast tumour with a leaf-like architecture and hypercellular stroma in an older woman is a:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Breast (resting.explanation: A phyllodes tumour has leaf-like fronds and a hypercellular stroma; it occurs in older women than fibroadenoma and can be benign, borderline or malignant (malignant ones metastasise haematogenously).

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Prostate Gland.question: Which two features identify the prostate histologically?
options: Two-cell glands with corpora amylacea in a fibromuscular stroma
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Prostate Gland.explanation: Two-cell glands with irregular lumina and corpora amylacea in a fibromuscular stroma identify the prostate.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Prostate Gland.question: The two cell layers of a benign prostatic gland are:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Prostate Gland.explanation: Benign prostatic glands have an outer basal layer and an inner luminal secretory layer.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Prostate Gland.question: Corpora amylacea are:
options: Benign lamellated concretions in gland lumina
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Prostate Gland.explanation: Corpora amylacea are benign, age-related lamellated glycoprotein concretions within gland lumina.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Prostate Gland.question: The histological hallmark of invasive prostatic adenocarcinoma is:
options: Loss of the basal cell layer
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Prostate Gland.explanation: Invasive carcinoma consists of malignant luminal cells lacking a basal layer (p63/HMWCK negative).

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Prostate Gland.question: Most prostate cancers arise in the ______ zone.
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Prostate Gland.explanation: Prostate cancers arise mostly in the peripheral zone, making them palpable on DRE.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Prostate Gland.question: Benign prostatic hyperplasia arises in the ______ zone.
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Prostate Gland.explanation: BPH occurs in the transitional/periurethral zone, compressing the urethra and causing obstruction.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Prostate Gland.question: PSA is a ______ that functions to ______.
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Prostate Gland.explanation: PSA is a serine protease that liquefies semen; it is the main serum marker for prostate disease.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Prostate Gland.question: A raised serum PSA can be caused by:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Prostate Gland.explanation: PSA is organ-specific but not cancer-specific — it rises in cancer, BPH and prostatitis.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Prostate Gland.question: Benign prostatic hyperplasia is driven by:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Prostate Gland.explanation: DHT drives the nodular hyperplasia of BPH, which is why 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors are effective.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Prostate Gland.question: Which drugs are used to treat BPH?
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Prostate Gland.explanation: Alpha-blockers relax prostatic smooth muscle and 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors reduce DHT-driven growth.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Prostate Gland.question: BPH characteristically causes:
options: Erectile failure as the first sign
Lower urinary tract symptoms (hesitancy, frequency, nocturia)
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Prostate Gland.explanation: Periurethral BPH obstructs outflow, causing hesitancy, weak stream, frequency and nocturia.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Prostate Gland.question: Prostatic adenocarcinoma histology typically shows:
options: Large glands with two cell layers
Small crowded glands with a single cell layer and prominent nucleoli
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Prostate Gland.explanation: Prostate cancer shows small crowded glands lacking basal cells, with enlarged nucleoli and perineural invasion.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Prostate Gland.question: Gleason grading of prostate cancer is based on:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Prostate Gland.explanation: Gleason grading assesses architectural patterns; the two commonest patterns are summed into the Gleason score.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Prostate Gland.question: Prostate cancer bone metastases are characteristically:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Prostate Gland.explanation: Prostate cancer produces osteoblastic (sclerotic) bone metastases, dense on imaging.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Prostate Gland.question: Prostate cancer spreads to the vertebrae via the:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Prostate Gland.explanation: The valveless Batson vertebral venous plexus provides a route for prostate cancer to reach the vertebrae.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Prostate Gland.question: Which basal-cell markers are used to distinguish benign from malignant prostate glands?
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Prostate Gland.explanation: p63 and HMWCK stain basal cells (present in benign glands, absent in invasive carcinoma).

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Prostate Gland.question: Why is prostate cancer often clinically silent until advanced?
options: It arises peripherally, away from the urethra
It arises in the transitional zone
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Prostate Gland.explanation: Peripheral-zone tumours do not obstruct the urethra early, so they are often silent until locally advanced or metastatic.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Prostate Gland.question: The prostatic urethra passing through the gland is lined by:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Prostate Gland.explanation: The prostatic urethra is lined by transitional (urothelial) epithelium.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Prostate Gland.question: Which zone surrounds the ejaculatory ducts?
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Prostate Gland.explanation: The central zone surrounds the ejaculatory ducts as they pass to the urethra.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Prostate Gland.question: Corpora amylacea in a prostate specimen indicate:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Prostate Gland.explanation: Corpora amylacea are benign, age-related luminal concretions and do not signify malignancy.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Prostate Gland.question: Which immunostain is positive in prostatic adenocarcinoma but negative in benign glands?
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Prostate Gland.explanation: AMACR (P504S) is positive in prostatic carcinoma; the basal markers p63 and HMWCK/CK5-6 are positive in benign glands and lost in carcinoma.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Prostate Gland.question: The recognised precursor lesion of prostatic adenocarcinoma is:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Prostate Gland.explanation: High-grade PIN — neoplastic luminal cells with a patchy basal layer — is the precursor of invasive adenocarcinoma; BPH is not premalignant.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Prostate Gland.question: In the ISUP system, Grade Group 2 corresponds to a Gleason score of:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Prostate Gland.explanation: Grade Group 2 = Gleason 3+4=7 (predominantly well-formed glands); GG3 = 4+3=7, GG1 = ≤6, GG4 = 8, GG5 = 9–10.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Prostate Gland.question: Testosterone is converted to the more potent DHT within the prostate by:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Prostate Gland.explanation: 5-alpha-reductase type 2 converts testosterone to DHT; finasteride inhibits it, shrinking DHT-driven BPH.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Prostate Gland.question: A man started on a GnRH agonist (leuprolide) for metastatic prostate cancer may initially experience:
options: Permanent sterility as the only effect
A transient testosterone flare that can worsen symptoms
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Prostate Gland.explanation: GnRH agonists first stimulate then down-regulate the pituitary, causing an initial testosterone flare before androgen deprivation; anti-androgen cover is given to prevent flare.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Prostate Gland.question: Carcinoma essentially never arises in which region of the prostate?
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Prostate Gland.explanation: The anterior fibromuscular stroma is non-glandular (smooth muscle and fibrous tissue), so carcinoma essentially does not arise there; most cancers arise in the peripheral zone.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.question: The ectocervix is lined by:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.explanation: The ectocervix has non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium, continuous with the vagina.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.question: The endocervix is lined by:
options: Simple columnar mucus-secreting epithelium with glands
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.explanation: The endocervical canal is lined by simple columnar mucus cells with deep branching glands (crypts).

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.question: The transformation zone of the cervix is:
options: The region of squamous metaplasia between old and new squamocolumnar junctions
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.explanation: The transformation zone is where exposed columnar epithelium has undergone squamous metaplasia; it is the key site of HPV disease.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.question: Most cervical cancers and dysplasia arise at the:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.explanation: CIN and cervical cancer arise at the transformation zone, where HPV infects metaplastic cells.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.question: A cervical smear is designed to sample the:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.explanation: The smear samples the transformation zone because that is where dysplasia and cancer develop.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.question: Cervical ectropion is:
options: Columnar epithelium everted onto the ectocervix
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.explanation: Ectropion is eversion of endocervical columnar epithelium onto the ectocervix under oestrogen, causing contact bleeding.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.question: Nabothian cysts form when:
options: Metaplastic squamous epithelium blocks endocervical gland openings
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.explanation: Nabothian cysts are mucus-retention cysts caused by squamous metaplasia occluding endocervical gland outlets.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.question: Koilocytes are a cytological sign of:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.explanation: Koilocytes (perinuclear halo, raisinoid nucleus) are the cytopathic effect of HPV.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.question: Which HPV types cause most cervical cancers?
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.explanation: High-risk HPV 16 and 18 account for most cervical cancers (6 and 11 cause genital warts).

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.question: HPV E6 and E7 oncoproteins act by inactivating:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.explanation: E6 inactivates p53 and E7 inactivates Rb, removing tumour-suppressor control.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.question: The commonest histological type of cervical cancer is:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.explanation: Squamous cell carcinoma, arising from the transformation zone, is the commonest cervical cancer.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.question: Cervical adenocarcinoma arises from:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.explanation: Adenocarcinoma arises from endocervical glandular cells; it is HPV-related but harder to detect on smear.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.question: The Schiller (iodine) test works because normal squamous epithelium is:
options: Glycogen-rich and stains brown with iodine
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.explanation: Glycogen-rich normal squamous epithelium stains brown with iodine; abnormal areas lack glycogen and stay pale.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.question: Cervical mucus under oestrogen (mid-cycle) is:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.explanation: Oestrogen makes cervical mucus thin, watery and fern-forming to facilitate sperm passage; progesterone thickens it.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.question: CIN differs from invasive cervical carcinoma in that CIN:
options: Is dysplasia confined above the basement membrane
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.explanation: CIN is intra-epithelial dysplasia (above the basement membrane); invasion breaches the basement membrane.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.question: Squamous metaplasia in the cervical transformation zone is:
options: A normal physiological adaptation, but the site of HPV vulnerability
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.explanation: Squamous metaplasia is a normal adaptation; however, the dividing metaplastic cells are susceptible to HPV and neoplasia.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.question: After menopause, the squamocolumnar junction typically:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.explanation: With low oestrogen the SCJ recedes into the canal, making the transformation zone harder to sample.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.question: Cervicitis is most commonly caused by:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.explanation: Cervicitis is often due to Chlamydia or gonorrhoea, causing discharge and contact bleeding.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.question: Which feature distinguishes the cervix from the uterine body histologically?
options: Squamous ectocervix + glandular endocervix with a mainly fibrous stroma
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.explanation: The cervix has squamous ectocervix and glandular endocervix over a predominantly fibrous stroma, unlike the muscular endometrial uterine body.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.question: Why is cervical adenocarcinoma more likely to be missed by cytology?
options: It arises higher in the endocervical canal, away from the sampled squamous TZ
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.explanation: Endocervical adenocarcinoma arises within the canal/glands away from the squamous transformation zone that the smear samples.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.question: Squamous metaplasia in the cervical transformation zone arises from:
options: Basal cells of the vaginal wall
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.explanation: Bipotential subcolumnar reserve cells proliferate and differentiate into squamous epithelium; metaplasia is not direct transdifferentiation of mature columnar cells.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.question: Diffuse "block" positivity of which immunostain confirms HSIL?
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.explanation: E7 inactivation of Rb causes feedback over-expression of p16; diffuse block p16 positivity is the surrogate marker of transforming high-risk HPV / HSIL.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.question: In the two-tier squamous system, HSIL corresponds to:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.explanation: HSIL = CIN2 and CIN3 (transforming infection, true precancer); LSIL = CIN1 (productive infection that usually regresses).

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.question: The modern primary cervical screening test in most programmes is:
options: High-risk HPV testing with reflex cytology
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.explanation: Primary high-risk HPV testing (with reflex cytology if positive) is now first-line — more sensitive than cytology alone and better at detecting adenocarcinoma.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.question: At colposcopy, 5% acetic acid causes dysplastic epithelium to appear:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.explanation: Acetic acid coagulates the protein-dense, high-N:C dysplastic epithelium, turning it acetowhite and guiding targeted biopsy; Schiller iodine leaves it pale instead.

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.question: CIN2 is defined histologically by immature dysplastic cells occupying:
options: The lower one-third of the epithelium
Up to the lower two-thirds of the epithelium
The full thickness of the epithelium
The stroma below the basement membrane
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.explanation: CIN2 = dysplasia extending up to two-thirds; CIN1 = lower third, CIN3 = full thickness (still above an intact basement membrane).

histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.question: The nonavalent (9-valent) HPV vaccine covers types:
histology__REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix.explanation: The 9-valent HPV vaccine covers seven high-risk types (16/18/31/33/45/52/58) plus low-risk 6 and 11 (genital warts); it is given before sexual debut.
